draftParagraphs: Japan lists the United States among countries whose nationals may enter visa-exempt for qualifying short-term stays. For most listed countries, the landing permission is 90 days. For U.S. citizens visiting for tourism or qualifying business, the U.S. State Department says the passport must remain valid for the full stay, a return or onward ticket should be available, and visitors may not work in Japan's local economy or change to another status while there.

For a planned stay over 90 days, Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs says travelers should follow a work or long-stay visa route; in principle, they should obtain a Certificate of Eligibility through the Immigration Services Agency before applying for a visa at the Japanese mission responsible for where they live. The right route depends on the reason for travel, and a Certificate of Eligibility does not guarantee that a visa will be issued. Paid work also needs the correct status even when a stay is shorter than 90 days.

Treat visa-free entry as a limited short-stay pathway, not a general permission for any trip. Study, residency, extended stays, and some business activities require checking the Japanese status/visa rules before booking. Transit depends on itinerary, airport, whether the traveler passes immigration, and onward-country documents; confirm with the airline and Japanese authorities.

Keep passport, itinerary, accommodation/contact details, and any required onward travel evidence accessible. Confirm the passport is in good condition and check airline document rules. Dual nationals should check which passport they must use for each border.

Visit Japan Web offers electronic immigration and customs declaration procedures. Check the live official portal and its manual shortly before departure to confirm what can be completed online, whether it applies to the traveler, and what must still be presented in person. Declare goods and follow customs and quarantine rules. Food, plants, animal products, medicines, and high-value items can have special restrictions. Check official rules before packing rather than assuming an item is allowed because it is for personal use.

Use the relevant operator's current route, fare, and disruption information. Allow extra time for transfers and the first/last mile, especially outside major corridors.

The Japan Rail Pass is valid only on defined participating Japan Railways (JR) services and subject to its current eligibility, purchase, reservation, and train-specific rules. It does not automatically cover every train, subway, bus, or private railway. Compare the full itinerary and current fare/pass rules before buying.

Taxis can help with luggage, late arrivals, or places without convenient transit; payment acceptance varies. Confirm destination in writing or on a map. Recheck the current advisory, local notices, and airline updates before travel because risk ratings and conditions can change.

Official U.S. guidance identifies earthquakes, typhoons, tsunamis, landslides, and flooding among hazards to plan for. Travelers should know their accommodation's evacuation instructions, monitor local alerts and weather, and follow Japanese authorities' instructions. Conditions can interrupt rail, flights, roads, and access to services.

Use normal precautions with belongings and when going out. Laws around drugs, medicines, identification, driving, and other conduct can differ substantially from U.S. rules and may carry serious consequences. Read current country guidance; avoid turning a general country overview into assumptions about every neighborhood or venue.

draftParagraphs: CDC's Japan Traveler View was last reviewed August 25, 2026; we rechecked it October 29, 2026. It asks travelers to check vaccines and medicines and see a health professional at least a month before departure. It advises travelers to be up to date on routine vaccines and COVID-19 vaccines for which they are eligible. It says to consider hepatitis A vaccine for most travelers (and recommends it for some higher-risk activities such as street-food eating or rural travel); recommends hepatitis B vaccine for unvaccinated travelers younger than 60, while unvaccinated travelers 60 and older may get vaccinated; and recommends Japanese encephalitis vaccine for people moving to or spending long periods in affected areas or frequent travelers. For shorter trips, JE vaccine is a consideration when activities increase exposure (for example rural outdoor activities or lodging without screens/air conditioning), and is not recommended for short-term urban-only travel. These are CDC recommendations to discuss with a clinician, not individual medical advice.

The Japan page currently displays a Level 1 “Practice Usual Precautions” Travel Health Notice that links to Global Measles, dated May 28, 2025. That is a global notice, not a Japan-specific measles outbreak alert. CDC says all international travelers should be fully vaccinated against measles with MMR under its international travel recommendations. Check the live notice list and its date again before publication or travel.

The same CDC page lists dengue, leptospirosis, hantavirus, tuberculosis, and tick-borne encephalitis among its non-vaccine-preventable disease topics. CDC recommends practical precautions such as avoiding bug bites and contaminated floodwater, using safe food and water practices, preparing for outdoor conditions and heat, avoiding contact with unfamiliar animals, and seeking medical care after animal bites or scratches. Its health-care planning advice includes checking insurance, considering travel-health and medical-evacuation cover, carrying a local-language card for conditions/allergies/medicine names, and carrying prescription copies.

Do not assume a U.S. prescription makes a medicine legal to import. Japan's rules depend on ingredient, classification, quantity, and duration. Some medicines require prior Import Confirmation or other authorization; some are prohibited or controlled. Check each active ingredient with Japan's MHLW before packing and before departure. Do not rely on a brand name alone.

U.S. health insurance may not cover care abroad. State Department guidance says travelers should check coverage; medical facilities may require payment up front. Consider appropriate medical and evacuation coverage for the trip and keep insurer assistance details accessible.

Observe signs and local instructions, ask before photographing people or private spaces, keep shared areas clean, and be considerate of noise and other travelers. The Japan Tourism Agency specifically promotes considerate photography, cleaning up, and avoiding large luggage in crowded places.

Remove shoes where requested and follow posted directions at homes, some accommodations, religious sites, and other facilities. On public transport, keep calls and noise low, queue where marked, and keep bags from blocking doors or seats. These are practical etiquette cues, not a claim that every place has an identical rule.

Onsen, bathing, religious, and other facilities may have specific access rules, including rules about tattoos or swimwear; check the facility before arrival rather than assuming a countrywide policy. Ask permission before entering restricted/private areas or photographing ceremonies and worshippers.

facts.title: Declare cash and check restricted goods before packing
facts.text: Before entering Saudi Arabia, check whether any luggage, gifts, cash, or controlled items need a customs declaration. facts.text: If you plan to work or study, check the visa required for that activity before travel. A visa-free short visit does not grant permission to work, teach, or study. Confirm the requirements for your exact activity with the Korean embassy or consulate serving your U.S. residence.

facts.title: Arrival card, immigration, and customs
facts.text: Most foreign visitors without a valid K-ETA must submit an arrival card. Korea’s free e-Arrival Card can be submitted during the 72 hours before arrival; valid K-ETA holders and some other groups are exempt. Follow airport signs for immigration, baggage, quarantine when applicable, and customs. Customs rules apply to goods and cash; cash declaration guidance is under review because official Korean and U.S. sources disagree.

facts.title: Country transport and navigation
facts.text: Intercity trains, express and local buses, domestic flights, ferries, metro, and taxis are common options. Services, schedules, payments, and accessibility vary by operator and region; rural and island routes can be less frequent. Korea Tourism Organization lists NAVER Map and KakaoMap for route search, KORAIL+ for KORAIL trains, and k.ride for visitor taxi booking. Check current coverage and payment support in each official app or provider page.

facts.title: Won and checking cash-declaration rules
facts.text: South Korea uses the won (KRW). Official cash guidance disagrees: Korea Customs describes a declaration requirement above US$10,000 equivalent in covered payment instruments, while the checked U.S. country summary says no declaration is needed. Contact Korea Customs before carrying a large amount and confirm the reporting process for your direction of travel. This fact does not resolve the disagreement or state that cash is exempt.

facts.title: Current advisory, laws, and weather risks
facts.text: The U.S. State Department lists South Korea at Level 1, Exercise normal precautions (issued May 28, 2025; checked November 3, 2026). It warns that demonstrations can disrupt services and that tensions on the Korean Peninsula can rise. Avoid demonstrations and follow local alerts. Drug laws are strict, and some U.S. prescriptions are restricted. Heavy rain and flooding can occur in summer; typhoons may affect the country from May to November. Recheck the advisory and forecasts close to travel.

facts.title: CDC vaccines, regional malaria, and care costs
facts.text: Check the CDC South Korea Traveler View and speak with a clinician about vaccines and medicines before travel. CDC recommends hepatitis A vaccine for unvaccinated travelers and identifies malaria risk in some rural northern parts of Incheon, Gangwon, and Gyeonggi provinces, including near the DMZ, during March–December. The malaria advice is regional, not countrywide. U.S. insurance may not cover care abroad; check coverage and consider medical evacuation insurance. Review medicine import rules before packing prescriptions.

facts.title: Dining and respectful conduct
facts.text: Tipping is generally not expected in restaurants. Follow posted rules at homes, temples, and other venues, including shoe removal and photography guidance. Customs differ by setting; observe local signs and ask when unsure.

facts.text: Ask your U.S. carrier about South Korea roaming, costs, device compatibility, and coverage. Local prepaid SIM and eSIM options are available from carriers including KT and LG U+; check the current plan, coverage, data and voice limits, device compatibility, and activation rules with the provider. facts.title: Voltage, frequency, and plug adapter
facts.text: South Korea’s standard supply is 220 volts at 60 hertz, with two round-pin outlets common. U.S. travelers generally need a plug adapter. A plug adapter does not change voltage: check each device label, and use a voltage converter or leave behind any device that is not rated for 220 V.

facts.title: Police, ambulance, fire, and U.S. Embassy
facts.text: Call 112 for police and 119 for ambulance or fire. The Korea Tourism Organization’s 1330 line provides multilingual travel information and interpretation, but is not a replacement for emergency services. The U.S. State Department lists +82-2-397-4114 for the U.S. Embassy in Seoul, including after-hours emergencies. Check live contact details before travel.
